passages.text: RAINBOW, a meteor in form of a party-coloured arch, appearing in the heavens when the sun shines upon rain falling opposite to it.

It is caused by the refraction of the sun's rays in the drops of rain, and their reflection from the back of the drops to the eye of the spectator, as was explained by Des Cartes and more fully by Sir Isaac Newton.

The colours are seven: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet; the red being outermost in the principal bow, which is seen at an angle of about forty-two degrees from the point opposite the sun.
A secondary bow is often seen above the first, fainter, and with its colours in reversed order, being made by two reflections within the drop.
Every spectator sees his own rainbow, since it depends on the position of his eye.
A rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection and dispersion of light in water droplets, producing a spectrum of light in the sky. It appears opposite the Sun.
The colours form a continuous spectrum. Newton divided it into seven colours, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, partly by analogy with the seven notes of a musical scale.
In the primary rainbow, red is on the outside. The bow forms a circle about 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the Sun.
A secondary rainbow, caused by two reflections inside the droplets, appears outside the primary bow; it is fainter and its colours are reversed.
Rene Descartes explained the rainbow's angle in 1637, and Isaac Newton explained its colours as the separation of white light.
A rainbow is not located at a particular distance; each observer sees a different rainbow, formed by different droplets.
Supernumerary bands, faint pastel arcs inside the primary bow, can only be explained by the wave nature of light.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: forty-two degrees, secondary bow, Descartes, Newton, seven colours.

suggestedQuestions: Why did the 1797 entry call a rainbow a meteor?
Does a rainbow really have seven colours?

Why did the 1797 entry call a rainbow a.answer: In 1797 'meteor' meant any appearance in the sky, so a rainbow counted [B1]. Wikipedia calls it an optical phenomenon [W1]. This is a change in language: the explanation of the rainbow itself is the same in both texts [B2] [W1].

Does a rainbow really have seven colours.answer: Not as a fact of nature. The 1797 entry lists seven [B3]. Wikipedia says the colours form a continuous spectrum, and that Newton chose seven partly by analogy with the seven notes of a musical scale [W2].
